One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has tried to defend party leader Pauline Hanson’s decision to meet far-right convicted criminal Tommy Robinson during a recent visit to the UK. Hanson and her colleagues have spent recent days clarifying, explaining or walking back headline-grabbing parts of the One Nation leader’s trip to Europe, including a podcast interview with Robinson. On ABC’s 7.30 program last night, Joyce first acknowledged Robinson had done “some things” that were “basically against the law” but went on to blame a “form of Balkanisation, where there’s not an assimilation” for “massive problems, and we saw that in Bondi”. The host, Sarah Ferguson, put to Joyce that Hanson was effectively endorsing a man with an extensive criminal record, who had been condemned by UK authorities for encouraging race riots and retribution against minorities.

My question to you, Barnaby Joyce, is: is that not a red line? I believe that there is not a condoning of every action of Tommy Robinson. During the interview, Joyce also said that he did not know who had bankrolled Hanson’s trip. Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Steph Convery with the main action. We start with Barnaby Joyce’s rather unusual interview with the ABC’s 7.30 last night, in which he attempted to defend some of the more controversial aspects of his leader’s trip to Europe, in particular Pauline Hanson’s podcast with Tommy Robinson, while simultaneously trying to fend off an apparently misbehaving dog. ---

730 host Sarah Ferguson was asking Joyce about his defection from the National Party and whether Hanson had dragged him “further into a place of intolerance and racial discrimination”. “Are you really comfortable with where she is taking you,” Ferguson asked a visibly frustrated Joyce, who then bellowed ‘SIT DOWN’ mid-answer. The mood again soured when Ferguson implored Joyce to answer the question rather than worrying about the dog. “Don’t be rude Sarah, or this interview will grind to a halt,” he replied. Earlier on Monday, Joyce and Plibersek clashed in a heated debate over Hanson’s Spotlight comments. During an interview with British far-right activist Tommy Robinson — aired as part of Sunday’s special — Hanson said Australia’s problems started half a century ago.

[Lähde: 7NEWS Australia | URL: https://7news.com.au/news/one-nation-mp-barnaby-joyce-snaps-at-dog-during-fiery-abc-730-interview-c-22604069]
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce lost his cool during a television interview for the second time on Monday, but this time his ire wasn’t directed toward the other side of the camera.

The former deputy prime minister started his day with a fiery Sunrise clash with Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek, and things didn’t get much better when the national broadcaster came calling.

Appearing on the ABC’s flagship current affairs program 730, a pet dog seemed to be the target of the 59-year-old’s latest outburst.

Know the news with the 7NEWS app: Download today

Joyce’s interview came in the wake of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s appearance on 7NEWS Spotlight on Sunday, during which the senator bemoaned the end of the White Australia Policy and voiced support for mass deportations.

730 host Sarah Ferguson was asking Joyce about his defection from the National Party and whether Hanson had dragged him “further into a place of intolerance and racial discrimination”.

“Are you really comfortable with where she is taking you,” Ferguson asked a visibly frustrated Joyce, who then bellowed ‘SIT DOWN’ mid-answer.

The mood again soured when Ferguson implored Joyce to answer the question rather than worrying about the dog.

“Don’t be rude Sarah, or this interview will grind to a halt,” he replied.

Earlier on Monday, Joyce and Plibersek clashed in a heated debate over Hanson’s Spotlight comments.

During an interview with British far-right activist Tommy Robinson — aired as part of Sunday’s special — Hanson said Australia’s problems started half a century ago.

“Well, it started in 1973 with Gough Whitlam. So they opened up and got rid of the White Australia policy,” she during the interview. Then they started bringing in the different migrants.

“And a lot of them couldn’t speak English, but they learned to speak English. But over the decades, as the governments have changed and different people they’ve brought in, and a lot of people come into Australia purely for the welfare system.”

After a clip of the comments was shared widely online, Hanson posted a video to social media in which she denied wanting to reintroduce the White Australia Policy.

“Never ever have I advocated that, and I don’t believe in it as well,” Hanson said.

Hanson said she was strong on immigration and wanted to bring the “right people” into the country “and people who want to assimilate”, admitting she doesn’t want to bring in people “from certain countries that want to wear the burqa”.
